records.wording: Marcionite readings adopted: "and destroying the law and the prophets" after "misleading our nation", and "and turning away the women and the children" after the tribute. Epiphanius states twice, in two scholia, that the text had these words in addition to canonical Luke's; NA27 cites both for Marcion (McionE); Roth: very likely. The rest of the verse is NA27. Epiphanius' own wording of it is a summary (Roth); NA27 cites McionE also for the omission of "our", which Roth leaves open, and it is printed.
records.western: "And destroying the law and the prophets" also stands in Old Latin manuscripts (e b c ff2 gat i) and a few Vulgate manuscripts; c and e have "and he turned away our sons and wives from us" at 23:5.

records.reason: Class U?: Pilate tells the chief priests and rulers that neither he nor Herod found him guilty: a paragraph with no attested verse (METHOD §4.3). Restored by method (METHOD §11): by its words, three printed verses point to it: 23:18 "release (ἀπόλυσον) to us Barabbas" answers an offer of release that only 23:16 makes; 23:20 "again (πάλιν), wishing to release Jesus" has no earlier wish without it; the attested 23:22 "a third time" repeats 23:14–16 almost word for word ("I found nothing deserving death in him; having disciplined him, I will release him"), and the second finding, between 23:4 and 23:22, is 23:14–15. By its mechanics: release offered three times answers the denial spoken three times (22:34; 22:57–60). Reading: docs/research/correspondence/word_by_word.md, chapter 21, test of 23:13–16; second_pass.md §2.

records.reason: 23:34b, the dividing of the garments by lot: Tertullian states that Marcion removed it, because of Ps 22:18, and builds his argument on its absence. Epiphanius' scholion 71 mentions the dividing, but it runs 23:33, 34b and 45 together in Matthew's wording and is a summary (Volckmar, Zahn, Roth). Tertullian's explicit statement is followed. 23:34a, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do", is printed by NA27 in double brackets as not part of its text (absent from 𝔓75 ℵ1 B D* W Θ 070 579 1241 a sys sa). Neither Tertullian nor Epiphanius cites it; Ephrem mentions the saying in an argument against the Marcionites (Comm. Diat. 21.3), which Roth rates as a possible attestation only. It is not printed.
The rulers and soldiers mock him; the inscription. A paragraph with no attested verse. Ps 22:7, 16 in Tertullian 4.42.4 is not clearly a reference to it (Roth).

records.reason: Class U?: The two criminals; "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom". A paragraph with no attested verse; its answer (23:43) is attested absent. Restored by method (METHOD §11): by its mechanics, the printed text states the law of the two, "one taken along, the other left" (17:34–35), and brings two evil-doers to the cross, "one on the right and one on the left" (23:32–33), without bringing them back. Here one demands that he save himself, and the other fears God, accepts his measure, asks to be remembered, and is taken "today, with me". It completes three strands of the final text: faith's "with you… to death" (22:33) denied (22:54–62) and here kept by the evil-doer; remembering (22:61 → 23:42 → 24:6–8); and "today" (4:21; 19:9). Reading: docs/research/correspondence/word_by_word.md, chapter 21, test of 23:39–43; second_pass.md §2.
